gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the makers' 'active' wattages come from different drive counts: QNAP's 10.81 W for the TS-233 is 'tested with drives fully populated' (two drives), the DS124's 10.69 W is from a 1-bay box with one drive, and UGREEN's 16.38 W for the DXP2800 is with one 2 TB HDD. So the TS-233 runs two drives on about the power the DS124 needs for one, and the DXP2800 will draw more than its label once the second bay is filled.
standout_why: I compared against the cited QNAP TS-233 hardware-spec page and the Synology DS124/DS223j compare page, plus the uncited DS223j spec tab. QNAP's page has the 'fully populated' footnote but no rival figure to set it against. Synology's power footnote only links to a methods article, and its only drive note ('Fully loaded with Seagate 2TB ST2000VN000') belongs to the noise figure. None of the pages turns the figures into a per-drive basis. ChatGPT's table lists the DS124 (10.69 W) next to the TS-233 (10.81 W) as if they were equal, but one has one drive and the other two. No result covers UGREEN at all, and UGREEN's lab figure uses one drive.
decides: This backs the TS-233 as the pick for a 2-bay NAS on 12 V. It is the only one whose maker states both a 12 VDC adapter and a full-bay test (10.81 W with both bays, so about 5.4 W per populated bay). It also takes the DS124 down from an apparent tie to a 1-drive option. The UGREEN DXP2800 also runs on 12 V (12 V/5 A), but its 16.38 W is a one-drive figure, so with two drives it draws noticeably more than the TS-233. Synology never publishes its adapters' DC output voltage, so the 'Verify adapter' cells stay open.

findings.label: Power adapter
findings.value: Minimum 48 W adapter, 12 VDC output, 100–240 VAC input
findings.note: The only maker in this set that states the DC output voltage on its own spec page.

findings.label: Operating power, typical (test condition)
findings.value: 10.81 W with both bays populated; 3.43 W in disk standby
findings.note: Footnote under the operating figure: 'Tested with drives fully populated.' The TS-233 has 2 bays, so that means 2 drives: 10.81 / 2 = about 5.4 W per populated bay. The page doesn't name the drive model or say where power was measured (wall or DC side), and doesn't say whether the footnote also covers the standby figure.

findings.label: Access / hibernation power, adapter
findings.value: 10.69 W access, 3.44 W HDD hibernation; 36 W adapter (100–240 V AC input; DC output voltage not stated)
findings.source_title: Synology Inc. product compare DS124 / DS223j
findings.note: The DS124 is a 1-bay unit, so whatever the test setup, the 10.69 W figure has at most one drive. Normalized, that is about 10.7 W per drive, against about 5.4 W per drive for the TS-233.

findings.label: Access / hibernation power, adapter, test note
findings.value: 16.31 W access, 4 W HDD hibernation; 60 W adapter (DC output voltage not stated by Synology)
findings.note: The power footnote only says 'For more information on how power consumption is measured, refer to this article'. The drive note 'Fully loaded with Seagate 2TB ST2000VN000 hard drive(s) in the idle state' is attached to the noise level, not to power. If the power test also had both bays filled, that is about 8.2 W per drive. Warranty: 2 years, extendable to 4 with Extended Warranty Plus.

findings.label: Lab power (test condition) and adapter
findings.value: 16.38 W drive access, 5.24 W hibernation, with ONE 2 TB HDD; 60 W external adapter, 12 V/5 A
findings.note: This is Starry Hope's account of UGREEN's lab figure: 'measured 16.38 W with a 2TB hard drive active'. A one-drive figure on a 2-bay unit, so with two drives it will draw more. The same page reports OCinside at about 7 W idle and 34.7 W peak under stress, with two drives in RAID 1. List price $389.99 on that page; I didn't check it against UGREEN's store.
